Refil Björnsson was a Swedish prince and a descendant of Ragnar Lodbrok, whose existence is uncertain but is mentioned in the Heimskringla and the Gesta Danorum. He was said to have flourished in the early Viking Age and played a role in the Viking raids and conquests of Europe. Björnsson's historical significance lies in his connection to the Viking Age and his potential influence on the development of Scandinavian society. His legacy is also tied to the Norse mythology and the sagas that tell his story.

The Heimskringla, a medieval Icelandic manuscript, describes Björnsson as a son of a king and a leader of the Vikings, while the Gesta Danorum, a 12th-century Danish historical text, portrays him as a prince who participated in the Viking Age raids. These accounts suggest that Björnsson was involved in the Viking conquests of England, France, and Ireland. His role in these events is still debated among historians, but his presence is confirmed by several historical sources.

Björnsson's significance extends beyond his military exploits, as he is also mentioned in the Viking sagas, which provide valuable insights into the culture, society, and politics of the Viking Age. The sagas describe Björnsson as a just and fair ruler, who was beloved by his people and respected by his enemies. This portrayal of Björnsson challenges the common stereotype of the Viking warrior and highlights the complexity of Viking society.

Björnsson's legacy can be seen in the modern-day Scandinavian countries, which continue to celebrate their Viking heritage. The Viking Age is an integral part of Scandinavian history and culture, and Björnsson's connection to this period is a reminder of the enduring impact of the Viking Age on modern society.
